storm.summary_layperson: No thunderstorms are on radar or in the near-term forecast — expect a quiet, mostly sunny evening around the cove with no severe weather threat.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No storms are around to test it, but the Sound's cooler water (72°F vs 81°F air, an 8°F gap) is running a moderate stabilizing layer that would blunt anything that did try to move in.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar is clean around Riverside as of the 8:19 PM scan — no storm cells, no approaching reflectivity. Instability is essentially nonexistent right now: CAPE reads 0 J/kg, and the HRRR model keeps it at or near 0 J/kg through the entire evening window, only inching up to a trivial 60 J/kg around midnight. Zero fuel means there's nothing for thunderstorms to work with tonight.

The Area Forecast Discussion from NWS Upton does flag isolated pulse storms as possible with the warm, humid airmass moving in, but the office's own language places any activity well to the west, near the NYC metro terminals, and notes the probability for thunderstorms has actually lowered for this evening. Bulk shear is a moderate 21 kt, which would matter if there were updrafts to organize — but with no instability, shear is a moot point tonight.

The cove's usual storm-blunting mechanism — a cool Sound water layer under warm inland air — is present and moderately strong (8.1°F air-water delta), but it isn't actively being tested since there's nothing approaching to weaken. Think of it as loaded but not fired.

Most likely outcome: a dry, mostly sunny evening with no thunderstorm risk for Riverside or the surrounding area. What would change the call: any AFD update escalating the isolated-storm probability, or CAPE building faster than modeled as the airmass destabilizes over the next couple of days per the AFD's own outlook.

Two active NWS products are unrelated to storm risk: an Air Quality Alert (ozone/haze, not severe weather) and a Heat Advisory that doesn't begin until tomorrow morning (Aug 6, 11 AM) and isn't in effect for this evening's window.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander

hourly.shift_note: light and variable, local eddy at RYC

wind.tactics_blurb: Wind stays light and unsettled through the window (2–5 kt), and RYC's own reading in the cove is diverging sharply from the regional flow — a sign of local eddying, not a pattern worth playing. Expect a drifter-class evening with breeze in fits and starts; don't commit hard to either side, and be ready for a postponement if it drops under 3 kt.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-wind evening, not a sea-breeze day, even though the ingredients look partway there: the air-water temperature difference is a healthy 8.1°F, which normally favors a thermal breeze. But the sea-breeze fraction across coastal stations is only 0.4 (and 0.0 inland) — well short of the roughly 0.6 threshold needed to call an active sea breeze — so the thermal signal never organizes into a real onshore flow. That gates this to a gradient-only regime, and with the regional airport-anemometer mean at just 7.2 kt, it lands on the light end (moderate gradient is 8-15 kt).

There's no strong geographic driver to favor either side of the course tonight. RYC itself is reading ENE (78°) at only 3.2 kt, while the broader regional ensemble median sits at SSE (149°) — a 71° split that's well beyond normal noise. That gap points to a local eddy or shelter effect right at the cove rather than a real directional signal worth racing off of; treat any single-direction call with caution and play what you actually see on the water.

Through the window, expect the flow to stay light and scattered rather than build or collapse cleanly — this isn't a thermal that collapses at sunset, it's already weak gradient flow that just keeps drifting in direction, and if anything gets more variable as the boundary layer stabilizes after dark. HRRR's own hourly forecast shows a slow veer from ESE (105°) in the early window to SSE (155-161°) by the second half, which is consistent with the regional ensemble but may not translate cleanly into the sheltered cove given the RYC divergence noted above.

For racing: most of the window sits in the 2-5 kt range, which is drifter/light-air-specialist territory, bordering on too light to race at all in the 20:00 hour. Fleets should expect a patient, low-pressure evening rather than a powered-up one, and race committees may need to watch for a postponement window around sunset if the breeze drops toward calm.
